claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was a Christian monk and ascetic who lived from approximately 345 to 399 AD.

Evagrius left Constantinople around 382, joined a monastic community in Jerusalem led by Rufinus and Melania the Elder, took monastic vows in 383, and then spent the rest of his life in the Egyptian desert at Nitria and Kellia.
The Scholia in Ecclesiasten (Scholia on Ecclesiastes) is a commentary by Evagrius on the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, consisting of 73 scholies.
The Scholia in Ecclesiasten was edited for the first time by Paul Géhin and published in Sources Chrétiennes 397 in 1993.
The Scholia in Ecclesiasten belongs to the texts recently discovered and was edited for the first time in 1993.

Evagrius's interpretation of Ecclesiastes is linked to his particular conception of spiritual life and the salvation of creatures, and he takes up elements from the biblical author that accord with his own monastic sensibility while modifying the general scope of the book.
Evagrius gives a discontinuous commentary made of generally quite brief notes, and the influence of Origen is felt here and there.

The notes become increasingly sparse as the commentary progresses, and the author seems to have given in to fatigue toward the end; the scholies become rarer starting from chapter 9 and stop at verse 10 of chapter 11, with the last chapter of the book left aside.

The text is preserved as a unit, in whole or in part, in four manuscripts: Paris. Coislin. 193; Sinait. gr. 461 (c. 1425), which is a copy of the preceding; Athon. Iviron 555 (14th century); and manuscript no. 3 of the Skite of the Prodrome (18th century), which is a copy of the Iviron manuscript.

The scholies are also preserved through an indirect tradition in exegetical chains (catenas), where they sometimes retain their authentic form and sometimes are reduced to a brief form going back to Procopius of Gaza; the Vatican chain contains 59 of the 73 scholies.

The Evagrian authenticity of the scholies is beyond doubt for the editor, supported by numerous arguments of internal criticism and by the testimony of the Epitome of Procopius transmitted in Vatican. Barberin. gr. 388, where several scholies are explicitly attributed to Evagrius.
